reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: Ohtani is the only player in baseball you have to scout twice — and both reads come back elite. On the hitting side, the contact quality is almost absurd: .416 xwOBA, 93.8 mph average exit velocity, and a 16.6% barrel rate all sit at 96th percentile or better, and a 15.4% walk rate rounds out a profile that makes .399 OBP look like a floor, not a ceiling. The one honest wrinkle is a 28.3% whiff rate — that's 31st percentile — but when you're barreling the ball at this rate and taking walks at that clip, pitchers are stuck choosing their poison. On the mound, a 98.0 mph fastball, 2485 rpm spin, and 30.9% whiff rate combine for a 2.68 xERA that would anchor a rotation; ValuCast projects him to .286/.399/.552 with 39 home runs as a DH, and the Statcast profile says that's not optimistic.

reports.name: James Wood

The one real tension in his profile is the 30.6% strikeout rate, which is genuinely ugly, but a 15.8% walk rate (97th percentile) means pitchers can't just attack the zone to expose him, and the projection (.261/.377/.501, 37 HR, 22 SB) reflects a hitter whose damage when he connects is so extreme it outweighs the swing-and-miss. The xBA sitting at .270 while xSLG is at .588 tells you exactly what kind of hitter he is: not a high-contact guy, but a monster when bat finds ball, and at 23, the strikeout rate is the one lever that could move this from star to MVP-level if it tightens.

reports.name: Nick Kurtz
reports.published_report: Nick Kurtz is a walking machine who can absolutely mash — a rare combination that makes him one of the more dangerous young hitters in the game right now. His 19.5% walk rate is in the 100th percentile, his 94.1 mph average exit velocity sits at the 97th, and his 18.4% barrel rate lands at the 97th as well; the contact quality is genuinely elite. The one real thing standing between him and stardom is a 36.5% whiff rate that checks in at the 3rd percentile — he draws walks at a historic clip because he knows the zone, but when he does swing at breaking stuff he can be put away, and that 30.6% strikeout rate is the number that will get tested as he sees better scouting. ValuCast projects .269/.403/.519 with 37 home runs across a full season — if the strikeouts stabilize even modestly, that projection is a floor.

reports.name: Bryce Harper
reports.published_report: Bryce Harper is one of the best pure hitters alive right now, and the Statcast profile backs that up without any asterisks — his xwOBA (.411) and xSLG (.558) both sit in the 98th percentile, meaning the underlying contact quality is genuinely elite, not a product of a friendly park or a soft stretch of schedule. The tension in his profile is that a 34.0% chase rate and 30.1% whiff rate (25th and 20th percentiles, respectively) are real swing-and-miss concerns, yet his 14.4% walk rate (93rd percentile) shows he's still forcing pitchers to come to him enough that the damage gets done anyway. The ValuCast projection (.274/.375/.518, 34 HR, 102 RBI over 680 PA) reads as a full-season bet on that trade-off holding — he doesn't need to be a disciplined hitter in the traditional sense as long as he keeps ambushing strikes the way the expected numbers say he does. At 33, the one thing to watch isn't the power, it's whether pitchers eventually exploit those chase and whiff numbers enough to tip the balance.

reports.name: Iván Herrera
reports.published_report: Iván Herrera is a catcher who wins with his eyes, and the Statcast profile backs that up loud and clear. His 13.0% walk rate and 15.7% K% sit in the 88th and 79th percentiles respectively — that's a strike-zone command profile most big-league hitters don't own, and it's why his xwOBA comes out at .361 (84th percentile) despite middling exit velocity and a 6.7% barrel rate that won't scare anyone. The disconnect between that xwOBA and a 47th-percentile xSLG tells you exactly what he is: a contact-and-patience catcher whose value lives in getting on base, not in driving gaps, and ValuCast's full-season projection of .260/.382/.416 with 20 HR over 692 PA reflects that profile honestly. At 25 behind the plate in St. Louis, the bat is already real — the question is whether the contact quality ever catches up to the plate discipline.

reports.name: Zack Gelof

The Statcast profile tells the story plainly: his 23.0% Chase % sits in the 85th percentile, but a .231 xBA and .298 xwOBA — both bottom quarter of the league — mean the plate patience isn't converting into results, partly because his 27.3% Whiff % bleeds away the contact quality. ValuCast projects a .264/.325/.464 line over 412 PA with 18 HR and 14 SB, which is a useful fantasy contributor, but the .391 xSLG tells you the power projection is doing some heavy lifting that the underlying contact metrics don't fully support. Until he starts punishing the strikes he lays off the chases for, the ceiling here is a speed-and-some-pop second baseman rather than a core piece.

ValuCast projects .352/.405/.461 with a .109 ISO across 215 PA, so the profile is built entirely on bat-to-ball skill and on-base value, not thump. The one thing that limits his ceiling is right there in the Statcast data: a 28th-percentile sprint speed (26.5 ft/s) means the contact advantage doesn't get amplified on the bases the way it would for a plus runner, and any defensive slippage at short becomes a real conversation. At 23, the question isn't whether he can hit — it's whether the power stays light enough that teams decide the glove-speed combo at short asks too much of the profile.

reports.name: Dustin May
reports.published_report: Dustin May throws hard — 96.9 mph fastball sitting in the 83rd percentile — and his walk rate (6.4% BB%, 79th percentile) is genuinely plus, the kind of command foundation a rotation arm can build around. The problem is right there in the contact quality: a 46.4% hard-hit rate and 90.0 mph average exit velo that rank 9th and 25th percentile respectively, which means hitters who do make contact are doing real damage, and his 21.7% whiff rate (22nd percentile) doesn't give him a way out of that hole. reports.name: Taj Bradley
reports.published_report: Taj Bradley has a frontline fastball attached to a back-end profile — 96.8 mph heat that sits in the 85th percentile for FB velo, but contact quality tells a different story entirely. When hitters do make contact, it's loud: 46.1% hard-hit rate and a 91.7 mph average exit velo that rank in the 10th and 3rd percentiles respectively, which is about as bad as it gets. The strikeouts are real (25.4% K rate, 26.3% whiff rate), but a 9.8% walk rate and a chase rate sitting at just the 35th percentile mean he's not finishing enough counts on his terms, and when hitters stay patient and put the ball in play, they're doing damage. ValuCast projects a 4.08 ERA over 162 innings — a solid rotation piece on paper, but the barrel suppression just isn't there yet, and until the command tightens or the chase rate climbs, he's living dangerously every time he falls behind.

ValuCast's current projection carries that through: .310/.391/.483 with 23 home runs across 692 PA, which is a legitimate middle-of-the-order line for a 34-year-old whose game is built on contact quality, not athleticism. The one thing that decides his outcome at this age is whether that bat-to-ball skill holds — and right now, there's no signal it's slipping.

reports.name: Brandon Lowe

The catch is a 34.8% whiff rate (6th percentile) that drags his xBA down to .243 and keeps the AVG and OBP (.239/.314 projected) modest for a middle infielder — the power is real, the swing-and-miss is just as real, and one of them is going to define how you value him. At 31 in Pittsburgh, he's a roster-construction piece: a second baseman whose bat profiles more like a corner, with elite contact quality when he connects and enough strikeout risk to make a full-season counting-stat projection feel volatile.

His 6.1 BB% sits in the 83rd percentile, genuinely elite, and a 95.4 mph fastball with 2374 rpm spin gives him real stuff to work with, but a 25.4% Chase% (8th percentile) and 44.9% Hard-Hit% (13th percentile) tell you hitters aren't chasing and when they connect, they connect hard — the 4.46 xERA reflects that honestly. The one thing that decides his outcome is whether the whiff rate climbs — at 22.9% (33rd percentile), he's currently more of a pitch-to-contact guy with a walk problem solved and a hard-contact problem very much open.

Coors Field is doing him a favor, and ValuCast's current projection of 24 HR with a .258/.306/.514 slash over 425 PA is probably close to his best realistic outcome in that park. The xwOBA of .311 (39th percentile) and xSLG of .448 underneath the surface suggest the projection is carrying some Colorado air; the contact quality alone wouldn't build that line. The plate discipline has to improve for him to hold a starting job long-term — until it does, you're buying a streaky power bat with a real hole in it.

reports.name: Will Turner
reports.peak_summary: Projection: low-end everyday regular with medium risk. The current bat shape is balanced over 225 PA.
reports.published_report: Will Turner is a walk machine who can't hit for average — and right now, that's actually working. The 23-year-old left fielder is posting a .395 OBP in AA despite a .202 average, built almost entirely on a 22% walk rate that translates to an estimated 14.3% at the MLB level, nearly six points above league average. That patience props up a .800 OPS that his .225 BABIP and 13 steals suggest could look meaningfully different once the balls start falling in; the ISO sits at .203 in the actual line, projecting to .152 against MLB arms — right at league average, so the pop is real if modest. The one thing that decides his outcome is whether contact improves enough to keep pitchers honest, because a hitter this dependent on walks can be neutralized the moment a zone gets expanded on him. Projection has him as a bench or platoon piece most likely, with everyday regular as the ceiling — he's cooling slightly in ValuCast's rankings, down 2 spots over the last three days.
